Sur Burj Al Khamis

سور وبرج آل خميس

A 19th-century wall and tower that once watched over its town. Restored in 2016, it is now a café, a small museum and a meeting place for the community.

The story

From lookout to living heritage

The fort was built as a lookout to protect the town and watch the land around it. Two centuries later, its walls hold a café, exhibitions and cultural evenings.

Al-Busaidi era
1800s

Built as a lookout

The Ministry of Heritage and Tourism dates the fort to the reign of Sayyid Said bin Sultan Al-Busaidi. It was built to protect the town and watch the land around it.

Then and now

Fort, castle, or both?

A community fort, not a castle

The sign at the gate says "Castle", but the official name, Sur wa Burj Al Khamis, means the Al Khamis Wall and Tower. Its wall and single entrance controlled who came in, and its towers let guards see danger early.

It has no grand living spaces or show of power, which a ruler's castle would have. Its multi-purpose rooms, barza and mosque show that defence and daily life went side by side.

Inside the walls

What you will find

Hosoun Café

A youth-run specialty coffee shop under traditional wooden ceilings.

Oman Post corner

"Stamps and Collectibles" displays stamps, souvenirs and exclusive books, beside local pottery and art.

Inner courtyard

Set up as a stage for events, with stairs to the top of the wall.

Museum and barza

A small museum on Al Musannah's coastal, farming and Bedouin life, and the barza where townspeople once gathered.

Identity tower

One tower displays symbols of Omani identity: the sword, khanjar, rifle and stick.

Mosque and family room

A historic mosque inside the walls, and a room where local families sell traditional products.

Heritage values · ICOFORT Charter

Why it matters

Ranked from most to least important today. Military value is not first: the fort's strongest values come from the people who use it.

1Social and economic

A heritage site that pays its way

Private investment turned the fort into a working café and venue. Visitor numbers grew from about 9,866 by April 2024 to 18,625 in 2025.

See the evidence

Hosoun Café and the productive families' room; five Omani staff at the café; visitors rose from about 9,866 by April 2024 to 18,625 in 2025.

2Memory and identity

A stage for Omani culture

Evenings on pre-Islamic Omani culture, Qaranqashouh celebrations, Omani Women's Day and a Ramadan art show with more than 38 schools.

See the evidence

32 events in 2025; a museum on coastal, farming and Bedouin life; a tower displaying the sword, khanjar, rifle and stick.

3Human and anthropological

Built for people, not only war

The mosque and barza show that prayer and gathering were part of the fort from the start. It still carries the name of the Al Khamis family.

See the evidence

A historic mosque inside the walls; the reactivated barza; an operator chaired by an Al Khamis family member; plans for a Quran school taught the traditional way.

4Architectural and technical

Small, practical, local

A modest walled enclosure in the Al Batinah style, with one gate and two towers. Some of what you see today is reconstruction.

See the evidence

A 1,751 m² enclosure; one main gate, al-Sabah; towers 9.6 m and 8.9 m high; restored with sarooj, stone and Omani wood; the smaller tower rebuilt.

Location

Where to find it

In the village of Burj Al Khamis, Al Musannah, just south of Al Shuaiba and about 4 km from the main road to Sohar.

Good to know

  • Parking, a café, rest areas and restrooms on site.
  • Ground floor is wheelchair friendly; the towers are reached by stairs.
  • Outdoor areas get hot in summer, so visit early or late in the day.
  • Check event dates before you go: the courtyard often hosts evenings.
